journalism series published in these pages on the quantity, educational quality and caste
inequality of Bihar’s labour force — the share of population either working or looking for
a job — offers crucial insights on the labour market challenges facing Bihar. While the
state is a laggard in terms of share of overall working-age population (15-64 year-old), it
has the highest share of what can be described as young workers in the 15-29 age-group.
Almost all of the anecdotal evidence suggests that an overwhelming share of the younger
part of this labour force either wants a government job or migrates outside the state for
mostly better-paying blue-collar work. Migration and the endless wait for an elusive
government job has robbed Bihar of its most important comparative advantage — an
abundance of cheap unskilled workers. If employed well — this would take a concerted
intervention from both the State and markets — Bihar could do much better in improving
income generation in not just things such as manufacturing but also agricultural
production.


Doing this, however, would require a recalibration of educational priorities in the state.
Bihar’s labour force is poorly educated compared with the national average. It should
make a stronger pivot towards vocational education (without compromising on higher
education facilities) so that students do not limit their options to the elusive government
job. This could hold more promise if implemented well for women, given the huge
unutilised potential in labour intensive manufacturing sectors such as garments
manufacturing. For a state that was the epicentre for Mandal politics and is known for a


fusion of caste mobilisation on the promise of representation for almost four decades now,
it is revealing that almost all social groups are over-represented in agricultural
employment and under-represented in manufacturing and private services. Primacy of
politics around reservations, even if well-intentioned or even radical in a state with a
history of entrenched feudal oppression, has failed to unlock upward economic mobility
for the so-called subaltern. Bihar, given its demographic dividend, is crucial for India’s
future growth. Exploiting this potential will require an honest alignment of politics to the
labour market realities, not mere poll promises.

II. I’m thinking about the mother in Tillie Olsen’s “I Stand Here Ironing.” The iron goes
back and forth, back and forth, and so do her thoughts, tallying up all the ways she was
and was not enough as a mother. When we read this story in a class I teach for mother
writers, we always talk about mom guilt, and how difficult it is to raise children in the
midst of fraught moments in history.


For the narrator in the story, it was the Great Depression and World War II. For us mother
writers who gathered this past Wednesday night in downtown Minneapolis, it is the
occupation of our city by federal ICE agents who are kidnapping and killing people in
broad daylight. When I found out that an ICE agent had shot Renee Good in the face just a
short drive from our home, I was pouring coffee and scrolling on my phone while my
three-year-old son raced cars on our living room couch five feet away. He called for me. I
set my phone down and pushed the tears off my face with shaking hands. I went to him.


Even as I did what I could, I felt that all-too-familiar guilt that mothers know so well, and
that mother, writer, and activist Tillie Olsen wrote about in her oft-anthologized 1956
story. “I will become engulfed in all I did or did not do, with what should have been and
what cannot be helped.” How could I not feel guilty for not doing more, when there are
mothers in my city whose children have been taken from them? Where, in this necessary
resistance and revolution, did I belong?


My own words wouldn’t come to me, so I borrowed others’. I started searching for
poems to pair with possible action items to print out and put in my Little Free
Library. Typing the poems made me feel better. While I cut them out, I read them aloud
to my son. Each time I finished one, he said, “Anulla poem.” Another poem. In the class I
teach, we read poems, essays, and stories by mothers from various time periods and
places. We write and we share our writing. We laugh and we cry. We heal. From our
voices and the voices of writers before us, we weave together a community of mothers
who raise their voices and inspire one another.


When I opened my car door to drive to class this week, I couldn’t help thinking about
Renee Good. About the prize-winning poem she wrote that was shared widely online after
her murder. About the image of her driver’s side door, the pocket overflowing with kids’
toys.

III. If it was happening to humans, you would call it genocide. The latest available census
data for Madhya Pradesh shows that it’s left with only 3052 donkeys, an awful 94%
decline since 1997. This ‘animalcide’, however, is not limited to one state or country. Two
major factors (urbanisation+mechanisation and Chinese traditional medicine market) are
severing the worldwide man-donkey relationship, which goes back 7000 years. That far
from grieving this loss, we are not even noticing it, reflects our fundamental alienation
from plants and animals, air and earth. To mourn is to begin to heal. And begin to do the
work of saving what we have been killing mindlessly.


It’s true that excepting regions like sub-Saharan Africa, socio-economic factors are
deleting donkeys’ traditional roles in agriculture and transport. Even if this was the only
explanation for the drastic shrinking of their population, it shows us to be a hideously


thankless species. How swiftly we are forgetting how deeply our ancestors – artisans to
merchants to administrators – depended on them. Until just a few generations ago they
powered the caravans that linked cities, and in more ancient stories they ferried our
prophets and gods. There’s a second, more unconscionable cruelty. Ejiao, or donkey hide
gelatine, is not new to traditional Chinese medicine and beauty products. But demand’s
shot up on the back of the country’s prosperity, a 2011 period drama, Empresses in the
Palace, and an ageing population. Even so, it wouldn’t be decimating donkey populations
across other countries if those were putting up meaningful defences.


A 2021 comparative analysis of donkey and mule populations by Stuart L Norris et al
finds that between 1997-2018 India’s decline at 74% has actually been worse than China’s
72%. One country’s actions seem active, the other’s passive. But the end result being the
same, obviously neither can take the moral high ground. And guess who’s taking it along
with the donkey? Poorer communities. Across the developing world, there are folk badly
hit by the sudden surge in donkey prices. Often, this translates into a painfully increased
workload for poor women and girls. Who cares, say the rest.

V. Over 10 years after the landmark NALSA judgment — it recognised a “third gender”,
affirmed trans persons’ fundamental rights and the right to self-determination of gender
identity — and five years after the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules,
2020 came into effect, trans persons in India continue to face discrimination. On October
17, the Supreme Court pulled up the Centre and state governments for “brutishly”
reducing the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 and its corresponding
rules to “dead letters” and exhibiting “a grossly apathetic attitude towards the transgender
community”. Jane Kaushik, a transgender woman, petitioned the Court after allegedly
facing discrimination and the forceful termination of her employment at two private
schools in Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat in the span of a year. The SC bench hearing the
matter constituted an advisory committee to assess the implementation of the Trans Act
and recommend a “viable equal opportunity policy… to be introduced by the Union and
state governments” within three months of the draft’s submission. For establishments
lacking their own policies, the Centre’s policy will be enforceable.


The creation of a panel to operationalise protections guaranteed in law is a welcome step.
But it speaks of a larger failure — the lack of political will to ensure that transgender
citizens can live a life of dignity and equality as guaranteed by the Constitution and
affirmed by the SC. The NALSA judgment and the Trans Rules mandate protections
against discrimination in employment, medical care and education for transgender
persons. Yet, implementation has been abysmal. For example, the Rules require
governments to build separate washrooms and wards in hospitals. Over three years past
the deadline, however, this remains a pipe dream. The Rules also mandated the
constitution of transgender welfare boards, which only 19 states and Union Territories had


done as of 2024; fewer still are reportedly functional. Across states, transgender persons
have had to move high courts and the SC after being denied access to medical care,
employment opportunities, and documents such as passports and graduation certificates
due to bureaucratic apathy and/or insensitivity.


The fact that courts have had to step in repeatedly to ensure that the rights of a vulnerable
section of the citizenry are not violated, reflects poorly on the executive. It is up to the
state now to ensure the implementation of the Rules and the committee’s policy
recommendations.

identity — and five years after the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules,

reducing the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 and its corresponding

facing discrimination and the forceful termination of her employment at two private
schools in Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat in the span of a year. The SC bench hearing the
matter constituted an advisory committee to assess the implementation of the Trans Act
and recommend a “viable equal opportunity policy… to be introduced by the Union and
state governments” within three months of the draft’s submission. For establishments
lacking their own policies, the Centre’s policy will be enforceable.


The creation of a panel to operationalise protections guaranteed in law is a welcome step.

citizens can live a life of dignity and equality as guaranteed by the Constitution and
affirmed by the SC. The NALSA judgment and the Trans Rules mandate protections
against discrimination in employment, medical care and education for transgender
persons. Yet, implementation has been abysmal. For example, the Rules require
governments to build separate washrooms and wards in hospitals. Over three years past
the deadline, however, this remains a pipe dream. The Rules also mandated the
constitution of transgender welfare boards, which only 19 states and Union Territories had


done as of 2024; fewer still are reportedly functional. Across states, transgender persons
have had to move high courts and the SC after being denied access to medical care,
employment opportunities, and documents such as passports and graduation certificates
due to bureaucratic apathy and/or insensitivity.

section of the citizenry are not violated, reflects poorly on the executive. It is up to the
state now to ensure the implementation of the Rules and the committee’s policy
recommendations.

X. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, meticulously constructs a framework of liability that
extends beyond the direct perpetrator of a crime, recognizing the grave danger posed by
collective criminality and preparatory acts. This is achieved primarily through the doctrines
of abetment, conspiracy, common intention, and common object, which together form the
bedrock of holding individuals accountable for crimes they facilitate, plan, or commit in
concert.


Abetment, under Sections 107 to 120, criminalizes the process of instigating, conspiring, or
intentionally aiding the commission of an offence. It is an inchoate crime, punishable even
if the abetted act does not occur, though the penalty escalates if it does. Distinct yet related
is the substantive offence of Criminal Conspiracy under Section 120A, which punishes the
very agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act or a legal act by
illegal means. The agreement itself constitutes the crime, marking a point where law
intervenes at the earliest stage of collective criminal planning.


When a crime is executed by a group, the IPC employs potent doctrines of joint liability.
Section 34 introduces the principle of ‘Common Intention.’ It requires a prior meeting of
minds—a pre-arranged plan—between two or more persons. When a criminal act is done
in furtherance of this shared intention, each person is liable as if they alone committed the
act. This is a rule of evidence that attributes constructive liability based on shared subjective
intent. In contrast, Section 149 operates in the context of an ‘Unlawful Assembly’ of five or
more persons with a ‘Common Object’ from among those specified in Section 141. Here, if
any member commits an offence in prosecution of this common object, every member is
vicariously liable. The focus shifts from a proven prior plan to membership in a group with
an inherently dangerous unlawful purpose.


In essence, while abetment and conspiracy address the roots of collusion before and during
crime formulation, Sections 34 and 149 address its fruition in group action. Prosecutors
often employ these sections in tandem, using Section 149 for mob violence and Section 34


for smaller groups with a proven shared plan, ensuring the legal net is cast wide enough to
hold all culpable parties accountable for their role in the collective criminal enterprise.

questions.stimulus:
XI. The foundation of the international legal order rests upon the binding force of
agreements between states, a concept enshrined in the ancient principle of pacta sunt
servanda. This Latin maxim, meaning "agreements must be kept," is the very bedrock of
treaty law, ensuring predictability, stability, and good faith in international relations. While
its spirit underpins all contractual diplomacy, its modern, definitive codification is found
not in historic peace treaties like the Paris Peace Treaty, nor in the Hague Conventions
governing the conduct of war, but in a dedicated framework for treaty law itself. The
principle is formally articulated in Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of
Treaties (1969), which states that every treaty in force is binding upon the parties and must
be performed by them in good faith. Even the UN Charter, in its Article 2, implicitly relies
on this principle for its authority, but the comprehensive legal formulation is the work of
the Vienna Convention.


However, the sanctity of treaties is not absolute. A higher tier of legal norms exists that
restricts what states may agree upon, even consensually. These are known as jus cogens, or
peremptory norms of general international law. These fundamental principles, from which
no derogation is permitted, are considered so essential to the international community that
they invalidate any treaty or agreement conflicting with them. The source of these norms is
not found in specific bilateral investment treaties or the resolutions of a political body like
the UN Security Council. While the International Court of Justice may identify and apply
them, it does not create them. Instead, jus cogens norms are derived from peremptory norms
of general international law, recognized by the international community of states as a whole.
Examples include the prohibitions on genocide, slavery, torture, and aggressive war. They
form an inderogable core of international law, representing its constitutional principles and
standing above the ordinary law of treaties governed by pacta sunt servanda. Together, these


two doctrines create a structured hierarchy: states are bound by their agreements, but never
by agreements that violate the conscience of the international community.

agreements between states, a concept enshrined in the ancient principle of pacta sunt
servanda. This Latin maxim, meaning "agreements must be kept," is the very bedrock of
treaty law, ensuring predictability, stability, and good faith in international relations. While
its spirit underpins all contractual diplomacy, its modern, definitive codification is found
not in historic peace treaties like the Paris Peace Treaty, nor in the Hague Conventions
governing the conduct of war, but in a dedicated framework for treaty law itself. The
principle is formally articulated in Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of
Treaties (1969), which states that every treaty in force is binding upon the parties and must
be performed by them in good faith. Even the UN Charter, in its Article 2, implicitly relies
on this principle for its authority, but the comprehensive legal formulation is the work of
the Vienna Convention.


However, the sanctity of treaties is not absolute. A higher tier of legal norms exists that
restricts what states may agree upon, even consensually. These are known as jus cogens, or
peremptory norms of general international law. These fundamental principles, from which
no derogation is permitted, are considered so essential to the international community that
they invalidate any treaty or agreement conflicting with them. The source of these norms is
not found in specific bilateral investment treaties or the resolutions of a political body like
the UN Security Council. While the International Court of Justice may identify and apply
them, it does not create them. Instead, jus cogens norms are derived from peremptory norms
of general international law, recognized by the international community of states as a whole.
Examples include the prohibitions on genocide, slavery, torture, and aggressive war. They
form an inderogable core of international law, representing its constitutional principles and
standing above the ordinary law of treaties governed by pacta sunt servanda. Together, these


two doctrines create a structured hierarchy: states are bound by their agreements, but never
by agreements that violate the conscience of the international community.

questions.stimulus:
XII. The Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act of 1936 provides the definitive statutory
framework governing the solemnization and validity of marriages within the Parsi
Zoroastrian community in India. This legislation establishes specific essential conditions
that must be strictly fulfilled for a matrimonial union to be legally recognized. A
foundational requirement is the absolute monogamous character of the marriage; neither
party can have a living spouse at the time of the ceremony, thereby prohibiting bigamy.
Furthermore, the Act stipulates minimum ages, requiring the groom to have attained twenty-
one years and the bride eighteen years, ensuring a baseline of maturity for marital consent.


A critical substantive condition pertains to the prohibited degrees of relationship. Schedule
I of the PMDA meticulously details a list of kin, based on both consanguinity (blood
relations) and affinity (relations by marriage), between whom a marital bond is legally
forbidden. This prohibition is designed to prevent incestuous unions. To formally attest
compliance with this condition, the Act mandates a unique pre-marital procedural step: the
parties must submit a sworn affidavit confirming they do not fall within these prohibited
degrees. This affidavit requirement is a distinctive feature of Parsi matrimonial law, serving
as a documented, legal safeguard prior to solemnization.


The core of a valid Parsi marriage is its religious solemnization. The ceremony must be the
traditional "Ashirvad", performed by a duly ordained Parsi priest in the presence of at least
two Parsi witnesses. This underscores the Act’s intent to preserve the community’s religious
and cultural identity within the legal structure. The priest’s role extends beyond the
ceremonial; he bears a statutory duty to certify the marriage certificate and transmit it to the
appointed Registrar. This registration is not merely evidentiary but is mandatory, and the
marriage is not fully constituted in the eyes of the law until this civil formality is completed.
Thus, the PMDA artfully intertwines sacred tradition with secular legal obligation. The
marriage’s validity is contingent upon the seamless integration of these elements: capacity


of parties, absence of prohibited relations, proper religious ceremony, and compulsory state
registration, collectively creating a binding marital contract under the special Parsi personal
law.

XIII. The debate on the Preamble within India's Constituent Assembly was a profound
philosophical contest over the nation's self-identity. One of the most poignant moments
arose when member H.V. Kamath moved an amendment to begin the Preamble with the
words "In the name of God." This was not a mere procedural suggestion but a deeply felt
plea to anchor the supreme document of the nascent republic in a recognition of the
divine, reflecting the spiritual ethos of many of its people. The proposal sparked intense
debate between those who saw it as essential for the document's moral grounding and
those who argued it contradicted the secular foundation being laid for a state that would
remain neutral towards all religions. After considerable discussion, the amendment was
put to vote and was defeated. The Assembly ultimately chose the more inclusive and
majestic formulation, "We, the People of India...," emphasizing popular sovereignty over
any specific theological reference. This decision underscored the Assembly's commitment
to a secular state while acknowledging the depth of the sentiment through the seriousness
of the debate itself.


The content of the Preamble, however, drew its core inspiration from a seminal internal
document. The trio of "Justice, social, economic and political" did not originate from
foreign constitutions like the Irish or French, but was directly and consciously borrowed
from the historic Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946,
and adopted unanimously on January 22, 1947. This resolution was the Assembly's first
definitive statement of aims, its moral compass. By lifting this precise phraseology, the
framers intrinsically linked the final Constitution to that initial pledge, ensuring continuity
between the Assembly's first aspiration and the Preamble's solemn promise. Thus, the
Preamble emerged as a uniquely Indian synthesis, born from internal compromise—as seen


in the rejection of a specific invocation of God—and internal inspiration, deriving its
foundational goals from its own earlier declaration of intent.

questions.stimulus:
XIV. In the realm of tort law, which provides redress for civil wrongs independent of
contract, several distinct actions protect fundamental rights to bodily integrity and property.
Among the most direct are the interrelated torts of assault and battery, which safeguard
personal security. Assault is the intentional act of creating in another person a reasonable
apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact. It is the threat itself, the poised fist
or the menacing advance with a weapon, that constitutes the wrong, even if no physical
contact ensues. Battery is the consummation of that threat—the intentional and direct
application of unlawful force to another person’s body. Any non-consensual touching, from
a violent blow to an unwanted kiss, can fulfil this element, provided it is done with intent
and is deemed offensive by societal standards. The law thus draws a clear line between the
fear of imminent harm and the actuality of physical violation.


Equally intrusive is the tort of false imprisonment, which protects an individual’s liberty. It
is established by the total, unlawful restraint of a person’s freedom of movement within a
bounded area, for any duration, without lawful justification. The restraint can be physical,
such as locking someone in a room, or psychological, asserted through apparent authority
or threats of force. Crucially, the confinement must be complete; the existence of a
reasonable means of escape negates the claim. This tort underscores the high value placed
on personal autonomy within the legal system.


Parallel protections extend to property interests. Trespass to land is the unjustifiable
intrusion onto another’s possession of real property. It is a direct interference, requiring no
proof of actual damage. Simply walking onto another’s land without permission, throwing
objects onto it, or allowing anything to encroach upon it constitutes the tort. The right
protected is essentially the right to exclusive possession.


Similarly, trespass to goods involves direct, intentional interference with the possession of
personal property. This can be as minor as moving someone’s bag or as significant as
damaging their car. The essence is the impairment of the possessory right itself. A more
serious wrong is conversion, which constitutes a deliberate act inconsistent with the owner’s
rights of ownership, so severe that it warrants forcing the defendant to pay the full value of
the goods. It is an act of usurpation—selling another’s goods, destroying them, or
fundamentally altering their nature—where the converter treats the property as their own,
thereby denying the true owner’s title entirely. Together, these torts form a critical juridical
shield for both personal dignity and proprietary dominion.

   realistically crafted prop gun at another actor from a distance of fifteen feet. The second
   actor is fully aware it is a prop and part of the scene. Based on the principles described,
   what is the most accurate legal assessment?

It constitutes assault because pointing any weapon, even a prop, creates a

options.label: b

It constitutes battery because the action represents a threatening physical gesture
           directed at another person.

options.label: c
options.text:
No tort has occurred, as there was no reasonable apprehension of imminent
           harmful or offensive contact under the circumstances.

options.label: d
options.text:
It could constitute false imprisonment by creating a situation where the other
           actor felt unable to move freely on stage.

XV. On March 11, the Supreme Court dismissed a plea by the State Bank of India (SBI) to
extend the deadline for providing details of electoral bonds purchased anonymously and
their encashment by political parties to June 30, 2024. A five-judge Bench headed by the
Chief Justice of India D.Y. Chandrachud gave the bank 24 hours, that is, by the close of
business hours on March 12, to provide the details to the Election Commission of India
(ECI).


The petition was filed in the aftermath of the Supreme Court’s verdict on February 15
striking down the electoral bonds scheme, where the Court had directed the SBI to furnish
details of the bonds to the ECI by March 6, 2024. These details were to include the date of
purchase of each bond, the name of the purchaser of the bond and the denomination of the
bond purchased. The ECI was subsequently ordered to publish all such information shared
by the SBI on its official website by March 13, 2024.


The court was also hearing a contempt plea filed by NGOs — Association for Democratic
Reforms (ADR) and Common Cause — against the SBI Chairman Dinesh Kumar Khera
that contended that the bank was deliberately trying to ensure that details of donors and the
amounts contributed to political parties anonymously were not disclosed to the public
before the Lok Sabha elections due in April-May. Analysis reveals that the BJP was the
scheme’s greatest beneficiary.


At the outset of the proceedings, senior advocate Harish Salve appearing for the bank
submitted that matching the bonds purchased and names of donors with the parties which
redeemed the bonds was a “time-consuming and complex” exercise. He explained that the
details were kept in two separate silos and not stored in a digital format.


But the CJI pointed out that the judgment had not asked the bank to “match” information to
ascertain who contributed to which parties and only wanted a “plain disclosure”. He
asserted that the SBI in its own application said that such information was “readily
available”.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Why did the Supreme Court reject SBI’s plea
seeking extension of time to disclose electoral bonds data? | Explained”, The Hindu.]

questions.stimulus:
XVI. Lobsang Tsering, my octogenarian fellow villager, was a voracious reader and
traditional knowledge keeper. Before he died in 2024, he made it his mission to give me a
clear sense of the social, political and economic histories of our village – the site of my
fieldwork for my PhD thesis on snow leopard conservation and tourism – and Ladakh in
general.


He would spend hours telling me who married whom and how those alliances had been
effected, offering me a sense of the kinship networks in Ladakh. Moreover, he would tell
me about the histories of the Namgyal dynasty, which ruled from 1460 to 1834, and of
Tibetan Buddhism, the faith followed by half the population of Ladakh.


He would educate me about the succession of Namgyal kings, which Namgyal king had
been afflicted by leprosy and how these medical tribulations had affected our village.


After some time, I realised that his stories did not have to say much about the century or so
of Dogra dynasty rule in Ladakh. More often than not, Tsering’s social and historical
vignettes dealt with the period before Dogra rule began in the 1830s.


Lobsang Tsering was not an anomaly. It would seem that contemporary Ladakh has blanked
out from its collective memory the period of Dogra domination in the region. This erasure


partly helps us understand the roots of the political movement for self-governance in
Ladakh.


Ladakh was an independent kingdom till the 1830s. But from the 1830s to 1947, Ladakh
was a colonised territory. Its colonisation began in 1834, when Gulab Singh of Jammu, a
commander of the Sikh empire, dispatched Zorawar Singh Khaluria to invade Ladakh.
Zorawar’s forces defeated the haphazardly organised defence of the region by the Ladakhi
king.


A decade later, the East India Company defeated the Sikh empire in the first Anglo-Sikh
war, during which Gulab Singh sided with the British East India Company. As a reward, the
Company signed the Treaty of Amritsar with Gulab Singh in 1846. For Rs 75 lakh, Gulab
Singh got the kingdom of Jammu and Kashmir, including the Ladakh region.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “In the devastating legacy of Dogra domination
are the roots of Ladakh’s anxiety for autonomy”, Sroll.in.]

clear sense of the social, political and economic histories of our village – the site of my
fieldwork for my PhD thesis on snow leopard conservation and tourism – and Ladakh in
general.


He would spend hours telling me who married whom and how those alliances had been
effected, offering me a sense of the kinship networks in Ladakh. Moreover, he would tell
me about the histories of the Namgyal dynasty, which ruled from 1460 to 1834, and of
Tibetan Buddhism, the faith followed by half the population of Ladakh.


He would educate me about the succession of Namgyal kings, which Namgyal king had
been afflicted by leprosy and how these medical tribulations had affected our village.


After some time, I realised that his stories did not have to say much about the century or so
of Dogra dynasty rule in Ladakh. More often than not, Tsering’s social and historical
vignettes dealt with the period before Dogra rule began in the 1830s.


Lobsang Tsering was not an anomaly. It would seem that contemporary Ladakh has blanked
out from its collective memory the period of Dogra domination in the region. This erasure


partly helps us understand the roots of the political movement for self-governance in
Ladakh.

was a colonised territory. Its colonisation began in 1834, when Gulab Singh of Jammu, a
commander of the Sikh empire, dispatched Zorawar Singh Khaluria to invade Ladakh.
Zorawar’s forces defeated the haphazardly organised defence of the region by the Ladakhi
king.


A decade later, the East India Company defeated the Sikh empire in the first Anglo-Sikh
war, during which Gulab Singh sided with the British East India Company. As a reward, the
Company signed the Treaty of Amritsar with Gulab Singh in 1846. For Rs 75 lakh, Gulab
Singh got the kingdom of Jammu and Kashmir, including the Ladakh region.

questions.stimulus:
XVII. Scan the headlines and you might think that Western economies are on the verge of
an ‘inheritance explosion’. Popular narratives warn of a looming ‘great wealth transfer’ as
baby boomers pass down trillions, and some commentators fret about a new era of
‘inheritocracy’ in which an idle rich class dominates by virtue of birthright. The storyline is
alarming: booming bequests funnel ever more unearned riches to heirs, widening inequality
and sapping economic dynamism. This notion fits a broader anxiety of our age, that
capitalism is hardening into a hereditary hierarchy, undermining the meritocratic ideal.


Yes, inheritance values are rising across the Western world. But this does not pose an
existential threat to the economy, nor is it necessarily a drag on growth. Far from being a
feudal relic that cements a permanent aristocracy, inherited wealth has changed in character
and scale over time. Its relationship with growth and inequality is more complex than many
assume.


For most people, inherited family wealth consists of a parents’ home or long-term savings.
Occasionally, it is a family enterprise, and when such firms survive not just a few years but
several decades, they reflect a form of entrepreneurship that thinks in generations rather
than quarters. Recent research on inequality also suggests that inheritance can, in fact,
reduce wealth gaps, as bequests tend to matter far more for less wealthy heirs. Taxing
inheritances may seem like a neat solution to curb inequality, but in practice inheritance
taxes have often proven inefficient and inequitable. As a result, many countries that once
relied on them have quietly abandoned these taxes in favour of more effective capital
income taxes targeting profits, dividends and realised gains, rather than wealth stocks and
bequests.


In this essay, we take a reflective journey through the latest evidence and historical trends
on inherited wealth. We explore how the role of inheritance has evolved over the past


century, how bequests affect the distribution of wealth within and across generations, and
whether inheritance taxation has a constructive role to play in a modern tax system. A
nuanced picture emerges. While inheritance is not without challenges, it often fosters long-
term investment and continuity, and attempts to heavily tax or curtail it have frequently
backfired. Perhaps instead of fixating on what is passed down, we should focus on
expanding who gets to build and eventually inherit wealth, through policies that spur
growth, entrepreneurship and broad-based opportunity.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Is inherited wealth bad?”, aeon.]
